source_lines.42: 1.1 **Product exterior and actual slopes.** Use the abstract product coordinates of $N$ to draw it as an unknotted solid torus in $S^3$. Let $A$ be the core of the complementary solid torus. Then $K$ is linked once with $A$ and $U$, while $A,U$ are disjoint meridians of $K$. The exterior of $A\cup K\cup U$ is  $X=P\times S^1,$  where $P$ is a disk with two disjoint interior disks removed. One way to see this product without a diagram is to remove $K$ first: its exterior in $S^3$ is $D^2\times S^1$, where the circle factor is the meridian of $K$; the two meridians $A,U$ are fibers $\{a\}\times S^1$ and $\{u\}\times S^1$. Removing their product tubular neighborhoods removes two disks from the first factor. The boundary tori are $T_K,T_A,T_U$, corresponding to the three boundary circles of $P$.  Write $h$ for the positive product fiber and $b_K,b_A,b_U$ for the three oriented base-boundary circles. In the usual meridian/longitude coordinates,  $\mu_K=h,\quad\lambda_K=b_K,\qquad\mu_U=b_U,\quad\lambda_U=h.$  The retained external torus is $T_A$; its solid-torus meridian in the original $N$ is $h$. Thus the two filling slopes are $b_K+fh$ and $h$, where $f$ is the integer framing on $K$ relative to the selected product longitude. All these are identifications of actual product annuli and circles; no homology-only recognition of a filled manifold is being used. [given, F1, F2]
source_lines.48: 4.1 **The remaining filling and boundary reconstruction.** Now fill $T_K$ along $b_K$. Its filling meridian intersects the compression body's meridian $h$ once. The filled, punctured solid torus is therefore a 3-ball. Explicitly, the unpunctured union is the boundary of $D^2\times D^2$: the pieces $D^2\times S^1$ and $S^1\times D^2$ are its two solid tori, and their meridians are the two product circle factors $h,b_K$. Thus it is $S^3$ with its explicit standard product smoothing. Retaining the already specified puncture removes an ordinary product ball from that standard sphere and leaves a ball, with the annular boundary part inherited from $T_A$ and the two disk faces inherited from $D$.  Finally restore the cut along $D$. This attaches one ordinary 3-dimensional 1-handle to that ball, along the two displayed disk faces. It is a solid torus. Its meridian disk is $D$, so its external meridian is exactly $h$. More precisely the ball-with-two-disk-faces just constructed has its remaining annular boundary in the original $T_A$ product coordinates; regluing these two product disk faces reconstructs the same $D^2\times S^1$ product neighborhood with the same annular side. Choose the product ball and the meridian disk in the original $N$ by cutting its specified meridian disk. The preceding product identifications match those cut coordinates and their annular side. They therefore give a diffeomorphism after regluing whose restriction to all of $T_A$ is the original identity. No arbitrary boundary diffeomorphism is discarded or extended by a classification theorem. Compatible corner smoothings are compared in their seam collars by the existing rounding lemma.  Combining this boundary-relative identification with the explicit framing-reduction map $\Phi$ proves the Statement for every integral $f$. [given, F1, F2, step 3.1] ∎

source_lines.105: 1.1 Put $Y=\operatorname{Rep}_Q(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$. The block description makes $Y$ an affine finite-type scheme. The block parabolic is $P_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}=U\rtimes L$ with underlying scheme $\mathbb A^u\times L$, where $L=G_{\mathbf a}\times G_{\mathbf b}$; hence $P_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}$ is affine and finite type, and it is smooth because $U$ is a vector group and each general linear factor of $L$ is smooth by [F5]. The quotient definition in [F1] makes $Y\to[Y/P_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}]$ representable: after base change by a scheme $T\to[Y/P_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}]$ corresponding to a $P_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}$-torsor $R\to T$, the pullback is $R$. Fppf-local triviality and [F8] make this torsor an affine scheme over $T$. To see that $R\to T$ is smooth, extend its structure group to $G_{\mathbf a+\mathbf b}$; the resulting $G$-torsor is a tuple of frame bundles of vector bundles $E_i$, while the reduction to $P_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}$ specifies subbundles $F_i\subset E_i$ of ranks $a_i$ with locally free quotients. Zariski-locally these sequences split and the bundles admit adapted frames, so $R\to T$ is locally $P_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}\times T\to T$, which is smooth by [F9] and [F10]; it is surjective as a torsor. For two underlying $P_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}$-torsors $R,R'$ over $T$, their equivariant isomorphism functor is fppf-locally represented by $P_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}\times T$, and these affine local representatives descend by [F8]. Fppf-locally trivialize both torsors, with their equivariant maps given by $y,y':T'\to Y$. The compatible isomorphisms are cut out in $P_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}\times T'$ by $g\cdot y=y'$, the inverse image of $\Delta_Y$ under $(g,t)\mapsto(g\cdot y(t),y'(t))$. This is closed because $Y$ is separated, and the closed subscheme descends effectively by [F8]. Thus the diagonal is affine representable. Effective descent of torsors with maps is obtained by descending their affine schemes, actions and compatible maps by the affine-descent argument in the proof of [F2]; that argument uses only affineness of the group and target, so also applies to this parabolic and to its vector subgroup $U$. By [F8], $[Y/P_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}]$ is an algebraic stack. Now, for each arrow $h:i\to j$, the free off-diagonal block is $\operatorname{Hom}(V_i^{\mathbf b},V_j^{\mathbf a})$; hence $Y\to \operatorname{Rep}_Q(\mathbf a)\times\operatorname{Rep}_Q(\mathbf b)$ is a vector bundle of rank $e=\sum_{h:i\to j}b_i a_j$. The kernel $U$ of $P_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}\to L$ consists of upper-right vertex blocks and has dimension $u=\sum_i a_i b_i$. [F1, F2, F5, F8, F9, F10, given, construct]

Conversely, a map from $X\otimes Y\otimes Z$ balanced in both slots factors uniquely through either parenthesization: first apply the universal property in step 1.1 to one slot, then to the other. Tensoring preserves its split epimorphic universal maps; the two balancing projectors commute because the two actions on $Y$ commute. source_lines.48: 3.2 The regular bimodule $A$ is a left and right unit. The action maps $A\otimes_A X\to X$ and $X\otimes_A A\to X$ are balanced. Their inverses are induced by the algebra unit $\eta_A$ and the relevant unitors. The action and unit laws show the two composites are identities; the triangle equation for these unitors follows because its two paths agree on the universal balanced map, so step 2.1 forces equality. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]
